In 2016, FBI Director James Comey confirmed that Hillary Clinton, as Secretary of State, maintained a private email server that contained classified information, including material marked at the highest levels of secrecy. Comey acknowledged that Clinton and her staff were "extremely careless in their handling of very sensitive, highly classified information."

Under 18 U.S.C. § 793(f), gross negligence in handling national defense information is a felony. The statute does not require intent—negligence alone suffices. Yet Comey invented a new standard, claiming that no "reasonable prosecutor" would bring charges because they couldn't prove intent.

  • Bryan Nishimura, a Naval reservist, was convicted simply for storing classified materials on personal devices—without any evidence of transmission or hostile access.
  • Kristian Saucier, a Navy sailor, served a year in prison for taking photos inside a nuclear submarine.
  • Reality Winner received over five years for leaking a single classified document.

The double standard is glaring. Clinton's defenders argue she didn't "intend" harm, but the law governing classified information exists precisely because negligence itself creates harm. Intelligence sources may have been compromised. Methods may have been exposed. Foreign adversaries almost certainly penetrated her unsecured server—FBI investigators acknowledged they couldn't rule this out.

During Hillary Clinton's tenure as Secretary of State, the Clinton Foundation received unprecedented donations from foreign governments, corporations, and individuals who had business before the State Department. The pattern is unmistakable:

Uranium One: Russian nuclear officials sought U.S. approval to acquire Uranium One, which controlled 20% of American uranium production. Arms Sales: A 2015 International Business Times investigation found that the State Department approved $165 billion in commercial arms sales to 20 nations whose governments had donated to the Clinton Foundation—a 143% increase from the same nations during the Bush administration.

UBS: After Hillary Clinton intervened to settle a dispute between the IRS and Swiss banking giant UBS, the bank's donations to the Clinton Foundation grew from less than $60,000 to approximately $600,000, and UBS paid Bill Clinton $1.5 million for speaking engagements.

Corruption doesn't require explicit quid pro quo documented in writing. It requires pattern, opportunity, and benefit. The Clinton Foundation provided all three. While Hillary made government decisions, her family foundation—which funded their travel, employed their associates, and enhanced their prestige—received tens of millions from those benefiting from those decisions.

Obstruction and Destruction of Evidence

When Congress subpoenaed Hillary Clinton's emails regarding Benghazi, her team deleted over 30,000 emails, claiming they were "personal." Her staff used BleachBit software—specifically designed to prevent forensic recovery—to destroy the data.

She also destroyed mobile devices with hammers.

These are not the actions of innocence. These are the actions of concealment. Under 18 U.S.C. § 1519, destroying documents to obstruct a federal investigation is a felony. Under 18 U.S.C. § 1505, obstructing Congressional proceedings carries up to five years imprisonment.

Martha Stewart went to prison for lying to federal investigators. Michael Flynn was prosecuted for false statements. Roger Stone was convicted for obstruction. Yet Clinton destroyed subpoenaed evidence and faced no charges.

The failure to prosecute Hillary Clinton isn't merely about one person escaping accountability—it's about what that escape communicates to every American.

When ordinary citizens see powerful politicians evade laws that would imprison them, they lose faith in the system. When young military members lose their careers for minor security violations while a Secretary of State walks free after hosting classified information on a bathroom server, they learn that rules are for the powerless.

This cynicism corrodes democracy. It justifies bad behavior. It tells citizens that justice is merely power exercised with a legal vocabulary.

Prosecuting Hillary Clinton wouldn't be persecution—it would be the uniform application of laws that already exist. It would demonstrate that America means what its founding documents proclaim: that we are a nation of laws, not of men.

Critics will cry "political persecution." But investigation isn't persecution when evidence warrants it. The case against Hillary Clinton isn't a matter of conjecture or partisan animosity. It's documented in government reports, FBI interviews, financial disclosures, and Congressional testimony. What's missing isn't evidence—it's will.

Imprisoning Hillary Clinton would not be vengeance. It would be justice, applied as it should have been years ago. It would restore faith in institutions that desperately need restoration.
